title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
hook: a red mango falls from a tree, and Vaisheshika finds six different kinds of thing in that one moment

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaisheshika, the atoms: the paramanu, partless, so it never comes apart, and the breaking that happens in the joints. Did something break, and did you see where? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.
screen: `THE BREAKING IS IN THE JOINTS.` · `SIX KINDS OF THING.`

segments.voice: A ripe mango lets go of its branch and drops into the grass. Thud. It took less than a second. Ask what happened, and the answer seems simple: one thing happened. A mango fell. Vaisheshika would gently disagree. It would say that in that one second you were looking at several completely different kinds of thing, all braided together so tightly you never noticed the seams. There's the mango. There's its red. There's the falling. And there are a few more, quieter ones, that you'd only spot if someone pointed. Today Vaisheshika points.
screen: `A MANGO FALLS. THUD.` → `ONE EVENT?` → `SEVERAL KINDS OF THING, BRAIDED.`

segments.voice: The Vaisheshika Sutra names its kinds of thing early on, and the word for them is padartha, which tradition explains as the meaning of a word. Anything that can be named and known is a padartha. There are six in the Sutra's list. Watch them in the mango. First, substance, dravya: the mango itself, the thing that holds everything else. Second, quality, guna: its red, its sweetness, its weight. Third, action, karma: the falling. Yes, the same word as karma, but here it means simply motion. Fourth, the universal, samanya: mango-ness, the thing this mango shares with every other mango, so that one word can name them all. Fifth, particularity, vishesha, the word tradition links to the school's name: what makes this mango, at the very bottom, not that one. And sixth, inherence, samavaya: the glue. The red doesn't sit beside the mango like a sticker. It's in it, belonging. Inherence is that belonging. Later writers in the school added a seventh: absence. The mango that's no longer on the branch. The empty place is real too. So here's what Vaisheshika is doing. It's not making the world complicated. It's teaching you to see the seams. At home, that turns out to be useful. Someone you love snaps at you. The person is the substance. The irritation is a quality, and it comes and goes. The snapping is an action, and it's over. When you can tell them apart, the snap doesn't have to become the whole person.
screen: `PADARTHA: WHAT A WORD CAN NAME.` · `SUBSTANCE, QUALITY, ACTION.` · `UNIVERSAL, PARTICULAR, INHERENCE.` · `LATER, A SEVENTH: ABSENCE.` · then, large: `SEE THE SEAMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the seams in one moment. Settle, and breathe. Choose something in front of you, a cup, a plant, your own hand resting on your knee. Name the substance: the thing itself. Name one quality: its color, its warmth. Is there any action, a movement, even a small one? Then let one person come to mind, someone who irritated you recently. Name the person. Name the mood they were in. Name what they did. Notice how the mood and the action can pass while the person stays. If you pray, you can hold that person, not their mood, before God. The bell holds the time.
Vaisheshika. A school that names the kinds of thing in the world: substance, quality, action, the universal, the particular, inherence, and later, absence.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. Today, when someone snaps, see the seams: the person, the mood, the action. Let the mood and the action pass. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn its list of categories, the padarthas, at the start of their study, and later Nyaya-Vaisheshika primers teach the list with absence added as a seventh.

match.prompt: the mango, in six kinds of thing — tap the pairs.
pairs: the red belonging in the mango

myth: in Vaisheshika, karma here means fate
in the list of categories, karma means action: motion, like the mango falling.
later writers in the school added absence as a seventh category
the empty place on the branch is real too.
the universal is what makes this mango different from every other
that's vishesha, particularity. the universal is what all mangoes share.

fork.setup: the mango has fallen, and the branch is empty. is the empty place anything at all?
options: no, there's simply nothing to talk about.
yes: later Vaisheshika writers counted absence as a real category.
fork.reveal: the Sutra's list has six; later writers in the school added a seventh, absence. the mango that's no longer there is something you can know.

original.note: Sanskrit: padartha, explained as the meaning of a word: whatever a word can name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a category is a box for filing things.
what it means: a padartha is whatever a word can name and the mind can know, and seeing which kind a thing is lets you see the seams.
what a scholar hears: Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.4 lists six padarthas; abhava, absence, was added as a seventh in later works of the school.

notes: Editor pass: padartha's 'literally, the meaning of a word' and vishesha as 'namesake' softened to tradition's explanation (claims rule on etymology); stock 'ordinary Tuesday' line replaced.
The six padarthas are listed at Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.4 in the commonly used recension (numbering varies); confirm the reference and that 'six' is stated there.
Abhava as a seventh category is attributed to 'later writers in the school' with no names or dates; confirm (often traced to Shridhara, Udayana, Shivaditya).
Padartha glossed as pada + artha, 'the meaning of a word': lexical; confirm.
The mango example and the 'snapping person' application are the writer's own illustrations.
